title: Theres No I In America (2)

jokes.text: 'No! I need a Previously on!' followed immediately by a character doing a straight 'Previously on 30 Rock' recap
jokes.setup: Character panics about not understanding the situation
jokes.punchline: The show literally gives her — and the audience — a 'Previously on' recap on command, breaking the fourth wall of TV convention
jokes.explanation: Sharp meta gag that weaponizes a TV convention as a joke. The show literally performs a recap on cue. Economy is excellent — the setup and payoff are nearly simultaneous. Works as both a structural joke and a character joke (Liz's chaos-induced confusion). Earns its 8 by being genuinely clever about the form.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Going somewhere, Lemon?' Liz: 'Nothing. Dammit!'
jokes.setup: Jack appears, catching Liz trying to sneak out
jokes.punchline: Liz's non-answer 'Nothing' — she answers the implicit accusation rather than the question — followed by immediate self-aware cursing
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-executed character beat. Liz's brain-to-mouth filter collapsing — answering the unspoken accusation — is very Liz. 'Dammit!' adds self-awareness. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: 'I need you to marry me so I don't get sent back to Canada! Really? Now you have a thing?'
jokes.setup: Everyone is rushing around with political emergencies; another character barges in with a personal crisis
jokes.punchline: Liz's exhausted 'Now you have a thing?' — acknowledging the show's pattern of everyone having a crisis simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Semi-meta joke about the show's structure — everyone always has 'a thing.' Liz's weary acknowledgment lands well. The Canadian deportation premise adds absurdist flavor.

jokes.text: 'Don't know why I'm so worried about bringing my marble collection to work.'
jokes.setup: A throwaway line of a character musing aloud
jokes.punchline: The immediate payoff: the marbles spill everywhere (implied by the 'Butterfingers!' line at 00:41)
jokes.explanation: A classic telegraphed-disaster gag. The ironic foreshadowing ('don't know why I'm so worried') combined with the immediate payoff is tight physical comedy. Works as a visual gag too — the marbles spilling mid-chaos is a background absurdist moment.

jokes.text: 'Butterfingers!' — marbles spill everywhere
jokes.setup: Character just said they don't know why they were worried about bringing marbles to work
jokes.punchline: Immediately drops them
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the marble setup. Structure is excellent — the gap between setup and payoff is only 4 seconds, making the irony land hard. Visual chaos of marbles everywhere adds physical comedy value. 'Butterfingers!' is a deliberately lame exclamation that adds to the absurdity.

jokes.text: 'Why do we have that?' — reaction to some absurd prop/visual in the office
jokes.setup: Something clearly bizarre is visible in the background or foreground of the scene
jokes.punchline: The question implies the prop is so strange that no one knows why it exists, which is its own answer
jokes.explanation: A reaction beat that depends entirely on the visual — without seeing what it refers to, the line is functional but incomplete. In context, it's a quick absurdist background gag typical of 30 Rock's chaos energy.

jokes.text: 'Jacksonville's naming their new airport Sized strip club after me. No bottoms!'
jokes.setup: Jack explains that Northern Florida loves Jenna
jokes.punchline: Jenna matter-of-factly reveals Jacksonville is naming a strip club airport after her, with the specific detail 'No bottoms!' delivered as a point of pride
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Jenna joke — the specific absurdity (an airport-sized strip club, named after her, with no bottoms) delivered with total sincerity. The 'No bottoms!' detail is the killer escalation. Extremely high character integration — this joke only works coming from Jenna.

jokes.text: Liz fails to name a single Obama accomplishment: '...the stuff Obama's been doing! Like, uh...' [beat] 'The one with the guy? It was at night, and I feel like he was standing near a fence...'
jokes.setup: Liz passionately advocates for Obama to Jenna
jokes.punchline: She cannot name a single policy or accomplishment — her best attempt is a vague impressionistic memory involving a fence
jokes.explanation: A beautifully observed political satire joke. Liz represents the passionate but uninformed liberal voter — she believes deeply but can't articulate why. 'The one with the guy? It was at night, I feel like he was standing near a fence' is a perfect escalating descent into vagueness. High character integration, strong structure (passion → complete blankness), quotable.

jokes.text: 'This country needs Mitt Romney.' / 'Like it needs a hole in the head!' / 'A head has five holes, and they are all needed.'
jokes.setup: Standard political debate rhetoric — 'like it needs a hole in the head'
jokes.punchline: Jack takes the idiom literally and corrects it anatomically, undermining Liz's rhetorical flourish
jokes.explanation: Jack's literal interpretation of an idiom is peak Jack Donaghy — dismissive, pedantic, and somehow winning the argument. 'A head has five holes and they are all needed' is delivered as irrefutable fact. The economy is superb — three lines, complete bit. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'Because there's no "I" or "me" in "America."' / 'There's both.'
jokes.setup: Jenna declares she won't be swayed because there's 'no I or me in America' — a mangled version of the team-sports cliché
jokes.punchline: Immediately corrected: there IS both an 'I' and a 'me' in 'America' — the episode title is itself the setup for this joke
jokes.explanation: The episode title joke, and it earns the meta-status. Jenna botches the 'there's no I in team' cliché by applying it to 'America' — but she's wrong, because 'America' contains both 'I' and 'me.' The correction is devastating in its simplicity. Perfect economy. High character integration — Jenna's narcissism accidentally proving herself wrong. This is one of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: 'If I'm gonna get political, it's gonna be to build a better country for Jenna Maroney. Someone who respects the human fetus and recognizes its value as a hair volumizer.'
jokes.setup: Jenna declares she'll only support whoever helps Jenna
jokes.punchline: She advocates for fetal rights exclusively because fetuses make good hair volumizers — a grotesque non sequitur delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The 'fetus as hair volumizer' line is genuinely shocking, absurdist, and darkly funny. It takes the most politically charged subject (abortion) and reduces it to a vanity product, which is exactly Jenna's character. High originality — this is a joke only this character in this show could make. The delivery (presumably earnest) makes it even better.

jokes.text: 'Like debate?' / 'Like DeBarge? I love DeBarge!' / 'No, Jenna, I said --' / 'I love DeBarge too, Jenna.' / 'Point, Jack.'
jokes.setup: Jenna proposes a debate format
jokes.punchline: Jenna mishears 'debate' as 'DeBarge' (the 1980s R&B group), Jack immediately pivots to agreeing with Jenna about DeBarge to score political points, Liz acknowledges he won that exchange
jokes.explanation: A layered gag: Jenna's mishearing, Jack's instant opportunism (agreeing about DeBarge to curry favor), and Liz's defeated 'Point, Jack.' Three characters, three distinct voices, one tight exchange. The joke has great structure — each beat escalates the absurdity. Jack's 'I love DeBarge too, Jenna' is the highlight: pure calculated manipulation disguised as enthusiasm.

jokes.text: Kenneth's absentee ballot backstory: 'Until this year, I wasn't allowed to vote because Reverend Gary said choosing is a sin. But then Reverend Todd said, "Reverend Gary is dead! Long live Reverend Todd!"'
jokes.setup: Kenneth explains why he's only now voting for the first time
jokes.punchline: The reason is a religious authority figure who banned voting, who was then replaced by an equally arbitrary authority figure who reversed the ban — the power struggle is revealed via hilariously pompous proclamation
jokes.explanation: Classic Kenneth worldbuilding joke — his small-town religious community is a cult-adjacent dystopia. The medieval 'Long live Reverend Todd!' proclamation applied to a mundane voting situation is perfectly absurd. High character integration.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Voting is a great American tradition. Like laziness or, eh...' [trails off, implying he can't think of another example]
jokes.setup: Tracy endorses voting as a great American tradition
jokes.punchline: His only comparison is 'laziness' — he trails off unable to name a second tradition, which itself becomes the joke
jokes.explanation: Tracy's trailing-off is character-perfect — his enthusiasm for voting evaporates immediately when he tries to contextualize it. The ellipsis does the comedic work. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: 'The Parcells have been in this country since we went berserk and murdered everyone at Roanoke.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth expresses pride in his family's long American history
jokes.punchline: He casually implies the Parcell family was responsible for the mysterious Roanoke colony disappearance — mass murder — delivered with the same cheerful pride
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The Roanoke colony is a famous historical mystery — Kenneth casually solving it by implicating his own family in a massacre, with total cheerful pride, is dark genius. The contrast between the warm patriotic framing and the horrifying content is perfectly executed. Highly quotable. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'Like how you must have felt four years ago when you finally got to vote for a president who looks like you.' Tracy: 'Black Shrek ran for president?'
jokes.setup: Kenneth makes a heartfelt comment about Obama looking like Tracy
jokes.punchline: Tracy's reference point for a Black public figure is 'Black Shrek' — not Obama
jokes.explanation: 'Black Shrek' is a brilliantly specific, strange, and inexplicable reference that only Tracy Jordan would produce. The joke works on multiple levels: Tracy's limited cultural frame of reference, the absurdity of the specific comparison, and the comic deflation of Kenneth's sincere moment. High quotability.

jokes.text: 'I forgot about that half-nerd.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth clarifies that he meant Obama, not Black Shrek
jokes.punchline: Tracy dismisses Obama as 'that half-nerd' — a characterization that implies he categorizes Obama as only partially nerdy, which raises questions about the full-nerd baseline
jokes.explanation: Economy is perfect — 'that half-nerd' does a lot of work in three words. It's a Tracy-specific insult that implies a whole internal taxonomy of nerd-levels. Character integration is strong.

jokes.text: 'Probably because I get all my news from social media. And I've been banned from all social media.' / 'You have? Why?' / 'Someone has to be the first person to make a joke after a celebrity dies.'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why he's out of touch with political news
jokes.punchline: He's been banned from all social media because he makes 'too soon' jokes when celebrities die — and he's apparently the FIRST, every time, suggesting he waits for it
jokes.explanation: Superb Tracy Jordan character joke. The concept of being banned from all social media specifically for being 'first' with celebrity death jokes is both absurd and darkly plausible for Tracy. The layering — he gets no news because he's banned, he's banned because of the very thing that would make him uninformed — is elegant. Strong originality and character integration.

jokes.text: 'I guess I was a little "too soon" with Andy Griffith.' / 'What did you say?' / 'I can't unhear it! I can't unhear it!'
jokes.setup: Tracy admits to making a 'too soon' joke about Andy Griffith
jokes.punchline: Kenneth (a known Andy Griffith superfan character) is so horrified by whatever the joke was that he physically cannot process it — the joke itself is never revealed, making the audience's imagination do the work
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The reveal of *which* celebrity — Andy Griffith, Kenneth's hero — is the perfect specificity. The joke we never hear is funnier than anything they could have written out. Kenneth's 'I can't unhear it!' reaction to an unsaid joke is a brilliant structural choice. High character integration for both characters. Rewatch value because you notice Kenneth's devastation more each time.

jokes.text: Dot Com enters saying 'Happy Election Eve! Obama 2012! The first African-American president ever to be up for re-election. Whoo!' / 'Historical!' [sic]
jokes.setup: Dot Com bursts in with Obama enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: He says 'Historical!' instead of 'Historic!' — the malapropism delivered with full confidence undercuts his grand statement
jokes.explanation: Mild joke — the enthusiasm and malapropism land softly. Not a lot of craft investment; it's more of a setup for the Pete/election storyline than a standalone gag.

jokes.text: Pete's karaoke analogy for why no one will be as excited about Obama's re-election: 'It's like when you do karaoke, and everyone's like, "That was a really good American Pie, Pete. You knew all the words." And then you put it on again. And everyone leaves because no one can top it.'
jokes.setup: Pete tries to explain why 2012 won't have the same magic as 2008
jokes.punchline: His analogy — doing 'American Pie' twice at karaoke — is painfully apt and painfully personal, revealing Pete's social obliviousness
jokes.explanation: The karaoke analogy is genuinely well-crafted — it works as political commentary AND character comedy (Pete clearly has done this). The detail that 'everyone leaves because no one can top it' is a perfect beat of self-delusion. Slightly long in delivery but earns its laughs.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I agree. You're the one using negative words like "without" and "negative".'
jokes.setup: Liz says she was hoping to get through the campaign 'without going negative'
jokes.punchline: Jack pedantically points out she literally used the word 'negative' (and 'without'), framing her as the negative one
jokes.explanation: Sharp Jack Donaghy wordplay — he wins the argument through pure pedantry, twisting Liz's words against her with surgical precision. The inclusion of 'without' is an especially nice touch, showing Jack's total commitment to the bit. Economy is excellent. Character integration is high — this is exactly how Jack operates.

jokes.text: The attack ad: 'In 2011, Liz said, "I hope Adele's voice recovers from her polyps." The same polyps Jenna had prayed for.'
jokes.setup: A political-style attack ad targeting Liz's friendship with Jenna
jokes.punchline: The devastating 'evidence' is that Liz wished Adele well — which conflicts with Jenna having prayed for Adele's polyps to destroy her voice
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly executed political ad parody that works on multiple levels: it satirizes attack ad logic, reveals Jenna's petty evil (praying for a rival's polyps), and uses Adele's real-life 2011 vocal cord surgery. The specificity makes it land hard. High originality for the attack ad format applied to celebrity jealousy.

jokes.text: The attack ad reveals what Liz says 'behind closed doors' — presumably showing her in an unflattering private moment (visual gag inferred)
jokes.setup: The attack ad promises to reveal what Liz says when she thinks no one is listening
jokes.punchline: The footage/image is apparently so damning that 'Really, Liz?' is the only response needed
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that depends entirely on what's shown — the transcript gives us only 'Really, Liz?' suggesting the reveal is visual. Functional joke in context, but unscored without the visual component.

jokes.text: 'Liz Lemon. Wrong on cuteness. Wrong on other bitches. Wrong for Jenna.'
jokes.setup: Attack ad builds to its closing statement, mimicking real political ad language
jokes.punchline: The attack ad criteria are 'cuteness' and 'other bitches' — perfectly absurd Jenna-world priorities dressed up in solemn political language
jokes.explanation: The attack ad parody lands perfectly. 'Wrong on other bitches' as a political position is inspired — it takes the real attack ad formula ('wrong on the issues') and replaces 'issues' with pure Jenna priorities. The rhythm mirrors real political ads exactly, which makes the absurd content hit harder.

jokes.text: 'Research indicates that ad is polling quite well with both manic and depressive Jenna.'
jokes.setup: Jack reports the ad's polling data
jokes.punchline: He segments Jenna's mental states as political demographics — 'manic Jenna' and 'depressive Jenna' as separate voting blocs
jokes.explanation: Clever satirical joke that uses political polling language to describe Jenna's psychological states as demographic segments. The clinical delivery ('polling quite well with') contrasted with 'manic and depressive Jenna' is perfect Jack Donaghy register. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'She's a slut monster, and one of gay America's top hags.'
jokes.setup: Liz argues Jenna is a liberal
jokes.punchline: Jack's evidence for Jenna being a liberal is that she's a 'slut monster' and 'one of gay America's top hags' — framed as political qualifications
jokes.explanation: Jack's willingness to deploy 'slut monster' and 'top hag' as political credentials, delivered with complete seriousness, is funny. The joke is in the framing — these are presented as neutral demographic descriptors. Strong economy.

jokes.text: 'She's aging, mean and rich. That sounds Republican to me.'
jokes.setup: Jack argues Jenna might be Republican despite being a liberal
jokes.punchline: His Republican criteria: aging, mean, and rich — a brutally reductive but pointed political stereotype delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: A punchy political observation. Economy is excellent — three adjectives do the work. Slightly less original than other political jokes in the episode, but the delivery (Jack agreeing with his own stereotype of Republicans) adds ironic self-awareness.

jokes.text: 'Having been shot and left for dead in three different deserts, pro-gun control.'
jokes.setup: Liz argues Jenna is pro-gun control
jokes.punchline: Jenna's pro-gun-control stance is justified by having been 'shot and left for dead in three different deserts' — the number three and the specificity of 'different deserts' is the escalating detail
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Jenna worldbuilding. 'Shot and left for dead in three different deserts' implies a whole (absurd, violent) biography that is never explained and doesn't need to be. The word 'three' and 'different deserts' does spectacular work — it implies repetition and geographic variety. Perfectly delivered as a political credential. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: 'Seven years I've been mentoring you, and I haven't been able to move you an inch.' / 'Herstrionics!'
jokes.setup: Jack accuses Liz of 'histrionics'
jokes.punchline: Liz invents 'herstrionics' as a feminist correction to 'histrionics'
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully compact and quotable portmanteau joke. 'Herstrionics' is the kind of word that actually sounds like it could exist, which makes it funnier than pure nonsense. Very Liz — she's making a feminist point while also being slightly ridiculous. Economy is near-perfect: one word does everything.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Yet you persist in this impotent emotional weltanschauung.'
jokes.setup: Jack lectures Liz about her persistent liberalism
jokes.punchline: He deploys 'weltanschauung' (German for 'worldview') in a casual sentence — the sudden register shift to obscure German philosophy is pure Jack Donaghy posturing
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack intellectual pomposity joke. The contrast between 'impotent emotional' (accessible) and 'weltanschauung' (deliberately obscure German) is the joke. Works because it's character-specific — only Jack would say this.

jokes.text: 'Good God, Lemon! Enough with the histrionics! / Herstrionics!'
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz to stop her 'histrionics'
jokes.punchline: Liz coins 'herstrionics' — a feminist portmanteau correcting the male-coded prefix
jokes.explanation: Elegant one-word joke. 'Herstrionics' is a genuinely clever portmanteau that does double duty as feminist commentary and Liz Lemon character comedy. Maximum economy — one word is the entire punchline. Very quotable.

jokes.text: The TOMS shoes joke: 'Every pair you buy, they give a pair to a child that was forced to work in a factory that makes these shoes. It's not great!'
jokes.setup: Jack mocks Liz's 'emotional' shoe purchase
jokes.punchline: Liz defends the shoes (TOMS-style buy-one-give-one), but reveals the uncomfortable irony: the charity gives shoes to the child workers who make the shoes
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp satirical joke about performative liberal consumerism. The TOMS model used to reveal its own circular absurdity (child workers get the shoes they make) is clever, dark, and rings true. 'It's not great!' is a perfect Liz understatement. High originality and strong earned-vs-cheap score — this joke has a real target and lands squarely.

jokes.text: 'I'm the one who's in a stable relationship, Jack. I like my job, and I am one punch away from getting a free deviled egg at that cool new deviled egg place!'
jokes.setup: Liz argues Jack should learn from her contentment with life
jokes.punchline: Her evidence of life success culminates in loyalty card proximity to a free deviled egg — the specificity of 'deviled egg place' as a pinnacle of achievement deflates everything that came before
jokes.explanation: The escalating anti-climax of 'one punch away from a free deviled egg' as life's greatest triumph is very Liz Lemon. The concept of a 'cool new deviled egg place' is inherently funny — deviled eggs don't have cool restaurants. The specificity elevates what could be a generic 'Liz has low standards' joke.

jokes.text: Liz: 'So maybe you should let me rub off on you!' Jack: 'You wish, you pervert.'
jokes.setup: Liz makes an innocent argument about Jack learning from her
jokes.punchline: Jack hears the double entendre in 'rub off on you' and calls her a pervert
jokes.explanation: A standard double-entendre joke — functional but not especially crafted. 'You wish, you pervert' is a good Jack line, but the setup (rub off) is too obvious. Gets a chuckle but doesn't push boundaries. Below-average originality for 30 Rock.

jokes.text: Liz begins her big speech and is interrupted by her phone playing 'Surfin' Bird' — she answers and it's her gynecologist asking if she left a bag of Burger King in his office
jokes.setup: Liz is about to make her triumphant closing argument to Jack
jokes.punchline: Interrupted by her ringtone ('Surfin' Bird' / 'Bird is the Word') and a call from her gynecologist asking about abandoned Burger King — the combination of specifics (gynecologist + Burger King + the question) is the joke
jokes.explanation: A beautifully absurdist comedic interruption. The 'Surfin' Bird' ringtone is funny on its own. But 'Did anyone leave a bag of Burger King in your office?' asked by a gynecologist, combined with Liz's complete non-reaction (she just takes the call), creates a perfectly layered absurdist moment. The question implies Liz eats Burger King at the gynecologist, which is revealed without being stated. Classic Liz Lemon world.

jokes.text: 'Oh, that old clock tower. Nobody knows what it's counting down to.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth reads about the Stone Mountain clock tower ballot initiative
jokes.punchline: He mentions the countdown clock with total acceptance — 'nobody knows what it's counting down to' — as if this is completely normal and requires no further investigation
jokes.explanation: Great absurdist worldbuilding — Stone Mountain has an apocalyptic countdown clock and nobody seems concerned. Kenneth's breezy acceptance ('that old clock tower') is the joke. The horror-movie setup used as mundane local governance is funny.

jokes.text: Mayor Debbie's pro-clock statement: 'Hey! I'm gonna take the clock apart myself, then put it back together. I wanna see how it works! My friend Jojo did it with a toaster, and it's still good. Let me do it!'
jokes.setup: The ballot initiative requires a 'pro' statement from the mayor
jokes.punchline: Mayor Debbie's argument for civic infrastructure repair is that she wants to see how it works, supported by the precedent of Jojo successfully reassembling a toaster
jokes.explanation: A good absurdist joke about the quality of small-town democratic discourse. Mayor Debbie's argument is identical to a curious child's — the 'my friend Jojo did it with a toaster' as civic precedent is inspired. The enthusiasm makes it land.

jokes.text: The Hermit in the Clock Tower's 'con' statement: 'Ain't nobody touch my clock! It's my wife, and this is where I do my sniperin'!'
jokes.setup: The 'con' statement for the clock tower initiative is written by the hermit who lives there
jokes.punchline: He declares the clock his wife, and reveals he uses it as a sniper nest — presented as a legitimate civic objection in official ballot language
jokes.explanation: The hermit's objection contains multiple simultaneous jokes: (1) a man married to a clock, (2) a sniper nest in a clock tower framed as normal, (3) all of this presented as official democratic process. 'This is where I do my sniperin'' is especially good — the possessive and the casual '-in'' suffix make it sound like a hobby. Highly original, strong structure.

jokes.text: 'To this day, I have to live with the fact that I cast the deciding vote that made "white" the newest flavor of Mountain Dew. But I guess that's just life in a Dewmocracy.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth reflects on the weight of voting responsibility
jokes.punchline: 'Dewmocracy' — Mountain Dew actually ran a 'Dewmocracy' campaign where fans voted for flavors, and Kenneth apparently swung the vote for 'white.' The pun pays off a real-world reference while being a perfect piece of absurd Kenneth lore.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Dewmocracy' is a real Mountain Dew marketing campaign, which makes the joke work on multiple levels: it's a pun, it's absurd lore (Kenneth feels guilty about a soda vote), and it uses the corporate marketing language against itself as political satire. The setup — Kenneth's grave civic guilt — applied to a Mountain Dew flavor is perfectly deflating. Highly quotable. The joke rewards viewers who know the real Dewmocracy campaign.

jokes.text: Pete trying to invite security guard Maria to an election party: 'Hey, Maria. Hey, it's Election Day! Huge party upstairs tonight. Just like 2008. I'll see you there?'
jokes.setup: Pete is desperately trying to recreate the magic of a 2008 kiss with Maria
jokes.punchline: His barely disguised invitation — using the election as a pretext — is painfully transparent, and Maria's polite deflection makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — Pete's desperation is clear and relatable in a painful way. Sets up the running Pete/Maria gag but isn't especially crafted as a standalone joke.

jokes.text: 'Welcome to the first and only debate of the Jenna-ral election.'
jokes.setup: The debate begins with a formal introduction
jokes.punchline: 'Jenna-ral election' — a pun on 'general election' inserting Jenna's name
jokes.explanation: A clean, tight pun — 'Jenna-ral election' is the obvious joke but executed well. Economy is excellent (two words do the work). Slightly predictable given the premise.

jokes.text: 'Today we choose the future for a woman "People" magazine once called "an unnamed friend of the deceased".'
jokes.setup: Formal debate introduction lauding Jenna
jokes.punchline: 'People' magazine's best description of Jenna was 'unnamed friend of the deceased' — she's so obscure that even her one celebrity mention is accidental and anonymous
jokes.explanation: A wonderful Jenna character joke — her claim to fame is being anonymously adjacent to a dead celebrity in a magazine caption. The joke perfectly captures her D-list status while she believes herself a star. 'Unnamed friend of the deceased' is a killer specific phrase. High quotability, strong character integration.

jokes.text: The timer sound for debate time is the national anthem playing in full — 'Oh say can you see... and the home of the brave'
jokes.setup: Liz is told when her time is up she'll hear a sound
jokes.punchline: The 'sound' is the entire national anthem — implying either the debate has an extremely long time limit or someone made a very poor choice of timer
jokes.explanation: A visual/audio gag that plays well on screen — the entire anthem plays while everyone waits. The joke is in the absurd inappropriateness of the timer choice. The implied duration (the whole anthem) suggests Liz gets an extremely long speaking turn, or the timer is completely wrong.

jokes.text: Jenna's response to reproductive rights: 'Do you want a bunch of old men behind closed doors deciding what you can and cannot do with your body?' / 'Ooh, and how do they tell me their decisions? Do I get shocked whenever I do the wrong thing?'
jokes.setup: Liz makes a standard liberal argument about reproductive autonomy
jokes.punchline: Jenna misunderstands the concept entirely, assuming the men behind closed doors control her through electric shocks — which implies a very different and disturbing lifestyle she apparently considers plausible
jokes.explanation: A sharp Jenna character joke — her misunderstanding of reproductive rights as a shock-collar control system reveals a dark personal history she considers normal. The implied backstory is funnier than the explicit joke. Strong character integration — Jenna's worldview makes this misunderstanding perfectly plausible.

jokes.text: 'Under Mitt Romney, the arts program at Traci Lords Middle School, where little Shauna is a seventh-grader, would be gutted.'
jokes.setup: Liz cites a specific school threatened by Republican arts cuts
jokes.punchline: The school is named after Traci Lords — the infamous underage porn star — presented as a normal school name with no acknowledgment of the reference
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock background joke — 'Traci Lords Middle School' is slipped in as a throwaway reference, trusting the audience to catch it. The contrast between the earnest political argument and the name of a notorious pornographic actress used for a children's school is darkly funny. Rewards attentive viewing.

jokes.text: Liz's anti-arts-funding argument that accidentally becomes pro-Romney: 'If arts funding was cut, within a short time, our schools would be producing no new actresses. And Jenna Maroney would get every part.' / 'That's my America. That's Mitt Romney's America.'
jokes.setup: Liz makes a liberal argument about arts funding to Jenna
jokes.punchline: Her logical chain ends with Jenna getting every acting role due to no competition — which Jenna loves — meaning Liz's anti-Romney argument has accidentally become pro-Romney for Jenna's purposes
jokes.explanation: The best structured joke in the episode. Liz builds a legitimate liberal argument about arts funding → it destroys careers → no new actresses → Jenna gets every part → 'That's Mitt Romney's America!' The ironic reversal is perfectly constructed. The callback 'That's my America' (a political ad trope) repurposed here is chef's kiss. The whole sequence shows excellent comedic architecture — each beat follows logically but arrives at a completely absurd conclusion. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Jack's Republican celebrity list: 'We have the coolest celebrities. Scarlett Johansson. Blake Lively. Jessica Biel --' [Jenna is impressed] / 'Wow. Those are all very beautiful women. Do you really want to be photographed next to them?'
jokes.setup: Liz brags about the Democrats' cool celebrities
jokes.punchline: Jenna's vanity immediately becomes a vulnerability — being photographed next to beautiful women terrifies her
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed debate reversal — Liz's strong point (celebrity endorsers) is turned against her by exploiting Jenna's insecurity. The pivot to 'do you really want to be photographed next to them?' is quick and sharp. Strong character integration for Jenna.

jokes.text: Jack's Republican celebrity counter-list: 'Craig T. Nelson, Chuck Norris, and Charlton Heston's skull.' / 'You'd be the only cool Republican.'
jokes.setup: Jack presents the Republican celebrity roster as a selling point
jokes.punchline: The list is Craig T. Nelson, Chuck Norris, and 'Charlton Heston's skull' — Heston is dead, so Jack is literally offering a skull as a celebrity; Liz's follow-up 'you'd be the only cool Republican' acknowledges the weakness of the lineup
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'Charlton Heston's skull' is the standout — matter-of-factly listing a dead man's skull as a celebrity endorser. The escalating absurdity of the list (Nelson → Norris → a skull) builds perfectly. Liz's follow-up acknowledging Jenna would be the only cool Republican rewards the joke with a capper. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I stopped you when you wanted to join that white tiger magic show. I stopped you when you tried to drive us into Lake Michigan because Scottie Pippen got married.'
jokes.setup: Liz appeals to Jenna's trust in her judgment
jokes.punchline: Her evidence of good advice includes stopping Jenna from driving into a lake specifically because a basketball player got married — an inexplicable specific emotional logic
jokes.explanation: The Scottie Pippen detail is inspired — it implies Jenna had a relationship with (or obsession over) Pippen, and her response to his marriage was vehicular self-destruction. The specificity ('Lake Michigan', 'Scottie Pippen') makes this land harder than a generic example. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Jack claims to own a Fuddrucker's with Scottie Pippen and says Liz 'looks like' Scottie Pippen
jokes.setup: Liz mentions Scottie Pippen as evidence of her friendship history with Jenna
jokes.punchline: Jack name-drops knowing Pippen personally (through a Fuddrucker's partnership), then inexplicably insults Liz by saying she looks like him
jokes.explanation: Jack casually owning a Fuddrucker's with Scottie Pippen is perfect absurdist character comedy — of course Jack has unexpected celebrity business partnerships. Telling Liz she looks like Pippen is a great comedic insult because it's so specific and non sequitur.

jokes.text: Jack's closing argument is complete incoherent political word salad: 'When our founding fathers first set out, time and time again, our nation horizon... prosperity... dreams... freedom. But the spirit... journey... destiny. Mitt Romney values. Jenna values. I've met people. For this generation and generations to come. Thank you, America.'
jokes.setup: Jack delivers his closing statement in the Jenna debate
jokes.punchline: His speech is pure political signifier words with zero content — a perfect parody of empty political rhetoric, delivered with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: A sharp political satire joke — Jack's speech is grammatically political but semantically empty. 'I've met people' and 'Mitt Romney values. Jenna values.' are highlights. The joke works because it sounds almost like a real speech. 'Thank you, America' as a sincere kicker is good. Strong structure.

jokes.text: 'Good God, those are load-bearing balloons! Everyone, run for your lives!'
jokes.setup: The debate ends with apparent balloon drop
jokes.punchline: The balloons are 'load-bearing' — a structural impossibility and architectural disaster that Jack treats as a genuine emergency
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable and original lines. 'Load-bearing balloons' is an inherently absurd contradiction (balloons cannot bear loads) delivered with complete urgency. The joke works on originality alone — nobody has ever written this line before. 'Everyone, run for your lives!' as a response to decorative balloons is perfectly escalated panic. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Tracy's advice to Kenneth on voting: 'Columbus thought he was in India! And did he worry about being wrong? No! He just called everybody Indians. And we still do it today! Why? 'Cause.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth is worried about voting without being fully informed
jokes.punchline: Tracy's inspiring American example is Columbus's confident wrongness — presented as a model of decisive action. 'And we still do it today! Why? 'Cause.' is the perfect anti-explanation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy Jordan speech. The Columbus example reframes ignorant decisiveness as quintessentially American — the dark satirical point is that American history is built on confident wrongness. 'Why? 'Cause.' is a perfect non-answer that somehow IS an answer. High originality, strong structure, very quotable.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Just like when we named this country after the fourth or fifth guy who discovered it. Amerigo Vespucci? Who cares? America!'
jokes.setup: Tracy continues his argument for voting without knowing what you're doing
jokes.punchline: Tracy points out America was named after Vespucci, who was the 'fourth or fifth' discoverer — the casual dismissiveness ('who cares?') followed by triumphant 'America!' is the joke
jokes.explanation: A good extension of the Columbus speech. Tracy's historical summary ('fourth or fifth guy who discovered it') is slightly wrong in a Tracy-specific way. The anti-climactic pivot from detailed history to 'who cares? America!' perfectly encapsulates his character and the speech's satirical point.

jokes.text: Jack: 'How do you sleep at night, Jack?' / Jack: 'I don't. I take thousands of micronaps during the day.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks the rhetorical question 'How do you sleep at night?'
jokes.punchline: Jack answers it literally and specifically — he takes 'thousands of micronaps' — implying he has literally hacked sleep itself, which is more disturbing than the rhetorical implication
jokes.explanation: A perfect literalism joke. Taking a rhetorical question at face value and answering it specifically — 'thousands of micronaps' — is quintessential Jack Donaghy. The answer is funnier than anything the idiom could imply. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I would rather lose with my head held high, partly because when I have it down, it looks like this...'
jokes.setup: Liz makes a proud statement about losing with dignity
jokes.punchline: She immediately deflates it with a self-deprecating physical observation — her head-down look is apparently so bad it needs to be avoided for aesthetic reasons
jokes.explanation: A self-deprecating visual gag that requires the actress to make a specific unflattering face. The joke is that Liz's noble speech is motivated partly by not wanting to be photographed looking down. Character-specific and physical.

jokes.text: 'To be perfectly honest, I don't like Mitt Romney. The man doesn't drink. How does he let a moment land?'
jokes.setup: Jack confesses he doesn't actually like Romney
jokes.punchline: His objection to Romney is entirely about social drinking — 'how does he let a moment land?' — implying Jack's entire emotional life and social grace depends on alcohol, framed as a legitimate criticism
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a contender for best in the series. Jack's critique of Romney — 'The man doesn't drink. How does he let a moment land?' — is extraordinary character comedy. It reveals Jack's entire worldview (alcohol as social lubricant and emotional architecture), it's a legitimate critique dressed as personal offense, and 'how does he let a moment land?' is a phrase that sounds like it belongs in another, more literary conversation. Extremely quotable. Near-perfect character integration.

jokes.text: Jack's childhood flashback: 'Boston. 1968. Latah, Mah! I'm goin' down the pahk to play ball! I sure love Americer! Almost as much as I love chowdah --'
jokes.setup: Liz attempts an emotional appeal by imagining Jack as a child
jokes.punchline: Jack-as-child is an extremely thick Boston accent caricature, delivering American patriotism in the most cartoonishly regional way possible, interrupted when 'adult Jack' realizes what's happening
jokes.explanation: The Boston accent bit works because Alec Baldwin leans into it hard — 'pahk', 'chowdah', 'Americer' — and because the device (Liz summoning Jack's inner child as an argument) is inherently absurd. The interruption when Jack notices mid-chowdah is a good beat.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Lemon, this kind of sentimental nonsense didn't work with Jenna. It certainly won't work with a man who didn't cry at "Field of Dreams", not even when the bank failed to recoup its investment in the farm.'
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses Liz's emotional appeal
jokes.punchline: He claims not to have cried at 'Field of Dreams' — but his specific objection wasn't the emotional reunion, it was the bank's uncollected debt. He DID almost cry, but at the financial subplot.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Jack Donaghy's emotional response to 'Field of Dreams' being triggered not by the father-son reunion but by the bank's failure to recoup its farm investment is perfect character comedy. It reveals Jack's entire soul in one sentence. The specificity ('not even when the bank failed to recoup its investment in the farm') is what makes this legendary — he KNOWS the financial subplot well enough to cite it as his emotional flashpoint. Near-perfect scores across all dimensions. Comparable in quality to the Snip Snap anchor example.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Fine. Enjoy your president. I'm moving to France!' / Jack: 'But you can't get a decent iced tea there. Forget it!'
jokes.setup: Liz dramatically threatens to move to France if Romney wins
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately kills the fantasy with the most mundane possible objection — iced tea quality in France
jokes.explanation: Jack knowing exactly how to deflate Liz's dramatic gesture — and being right about the iced tea (France is famously bad at iced tea) — is great Jack-Liz chemistry. The specificity of iced tea over everything else Jack could object to is character-perfect.

jokes.text: Pete to NBC election anchor: 'Williams, I need you to call it for Obama right now! Remember that time you got a haircut, and I was the first person to say, "Someone got a haircut"? You owe me!'
jokes.setup: Pete desperately wants the election called before 6pm for Maria-related reasons
jokes.punchline: His leverage over the election anchor is having been the first to notice his haircut — the least bankable possible social debt, deployed with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: Pete's attempt to cash in a haircut observation as political currency is inspired. The specificity of 'I was the first person to say, Someone got a haircut' as a favor owed is very funny — it's the smallest imaginable social debt deployed for the largest imaginable political outcome. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'Everyone has to vote immediately! This election has to be over by six!' — Pete running through the office
jokes.setup: Pete is trying to get the election called early so Maria will still be on shift
jokes.punchline: His civic urgency is entirely motivated by a crush — he's trying to manipulate a national election for a date
jokes.explanation: Running gag continuation. The joke is in the incongruity of Pete's desperate urgency applied to a national election for personal romantic reasons. Mildly funny but functional.

jokes.text: The election anchor's response to Pete: 'Look, get a hobby, like me and my gymnastics!' [implied visual of anchor doing gymnastics]
jokes.setup: The anchor dismisses Pete's request
jokes.punchline: He reveals his hobby is gymnastics — and apparently demonstrates it — which is completely incongruous with the anchor's professional gravitas
jokes.explanation: A good visual gag — the solemn news anchor being revealed as a gymnastics enthusiast mid-broadcast. Depends partly on the visual for its full impact but works in transcript form as an absurdist non sequitur.

jokes.text: Pete's Joni Mitchell impression: 'If Joni Mitchell were here, she'd be like: [singing] "The big man won't give peace a chance / The cobblestones, cobblestones"'
jokes.setup: Pete is despairing about the election and life
jokes.punchline: He performs an original fake Joni Mitchell song that sounds vaguely like her style but with nonsense political lyrics, complete with the specific 'cobblestones, cobblestones' repetition
jokes.explanation: Pete's impromptu Joni Mitchell impression lands as character comedy — the desperation, the specific choice of Mitchell, and the half-coherent lyrics ('cobblestones, cobblestones') all paint a picture of a man losing it. The repetition of 'cobblestones' mimics Mitchell's actual style enough to be funny.

jokes.text: Coworker: 'Seriously, dude, let it go. It was just one kiss.' / Pete: 'Yeah, if you need a kiss so bad, why don't you kiss a potato like the rest of us?'
jokes.setup: Pete is told to let go of the Maria kiss
jokes.punchline: Pete's comeback implies that potato-kissing is a universal and normal alternative to human affection — 'like the rest of us'
jokes.explanation: Pete's potato comment is absurdist gold. 'Kiss a potato like the rest of us' implies that potato-kissing is a common, shared practice among their social circle, which is both deeply weird and strangely plausible for TGS's workplace culture. The 'like the rest of us' is the key escalator — it normalizes the bizarre.

jokes.text: Pete's speech: 'That night in 2008, everything felt possible. Like my whole life was ahead of me. I was gonna drive a sports car and say cool stuff like, "Wiki-what?"! And none of that has happened!'
jokes.setup: Pete delivers an impassioned speech about the hope of 2008
jokes.punchline: His vision of the future was to drive a sports car and say 'Wiki-what?' — the specific, dated, and pathetic nature of this aspiration deflates the speech beautifully
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Pete's grand vision of 2008 hope collapsing into 'drive a sports car and say Wiki-what?' is perfect character comedy. 'Wiki-what?' is so specifically 2008-internet-slang-adjacent that it's already dated by 2012, which makes his failure to achieve it even sadder. The emotional sincerity sells the deflation. High quotability — this line encapsulates Pete's entire life trajectory.

jokes.text: Pete's speech: 'I was gonna drive a sports car and say cool stuff like Wiki-what?! And none of that has happened!'
jokes.setup: Pete explains that the 2008 Obama kiss symbolized unlimited possibility
jokes.punchline: His specific vision of his transformed life: driving a sports car and saying 'Wiki-what?' — an extremely dated 2008 internet slang that further emphasizes how stuck he is
jokes.explanation: 'Wiki-what?' as Pete's aspiration for a cool catchphrase is perfectly pathetic — he imagined himself as someone who says things like that, and it's already obsolete. Good character joke with an excellent specific detail.

jokes.text: 'Nothing has changed! For Pete or America! And if we can't get that feeling back tonight for Pete's sake, when will we ever gonna get it back? For Pete's sake.'
jokes.setup: Emotional speech about Pete's connection to America's political hope
jokes.punchline: 'For Pete's sake' used as both a common idiom AND a literal reference to Pete the character — the double meaning lands at the emotional climax
jokes.explanation: A well-earned pun at an emotional moment — using 'for Pete's sake' literally (for the benefit of Pete Hornberger) while deploying it as the common exclamation. The repetition at the end ('For Pete's sake.' alone, as a beat) gives it weight. Good structure.

jokes.text: Jenna in a Twitter war with a spambot: 'Screw you, Dona-one-d Estaluj. I don't need Viagra! You need Viagra!'
jokes.setup: Jack asks Jenna to tweet her endorsement
jokes.punchline: Jenna is in the middle of a heated argument with a spam email name, yelling about Viagra — the mispronunciation of the spam name and her genuine fury make it perfect
jokes.explanation: Jenna engaging in genuine Twitter beef with a Viagra spambot — and clearly losing the argument — is perfectly in character. 'Dona-one-d Estaluj' is a great rendering of how a spam email name looks. Her sincere fury ('You need Viagra!') at a bot reveals her as both technologically illiterate and magnificently committed. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Mitt. It stands for Motorized Intelligent Technodrome Termina --' / [interrupted] 'It's a human's name.'
jokes.setup: Jenna asks if 'Mitt' is an acronym (calling him 'Mike Romney')
jokes.punchline: Jack begins inventing an elaborate acronym for 'Mitt' mid-sentence ('Motorized Intelligent Technodrome Termina--') before being cut off by the correct answer that it's just a name
jokes.explanation: The joke is Jack's split-second attempt to spin an acronym for 'Mitt' — and he gets surprisingly far ('Motorized Intelligent Technodrome') before being cut off. The reference to 'Technodrome' (from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles) implies this is the best Jack could do under pressure, which is funny given his intelligence. The interruption is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: 'No, my role model is Sara Blakely, the billionaire founder of Spanx. She's a genius. It's just kids' bike shorts for fatties!'
jokes.setup: A young girl mentions her role model, Sara Blakely
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'clarification' of Spanx — 'it's just kids' bike shorts for fatties' — delivered as genuine business analysis
jokes.explanation: Jack Donaghy reducing a billion-dollar brand to 'kids' bike shorts for fatties' with total analytical confidence is very in character. The reductive accuracy is the joke — he's not wrong about the basic concept, just devastatingly blunt. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: 'When I was a boy, I used to go to Fenway and sell my urine... for fans to throw at Mickey Mantle.'
jokes.setup: Jack bonds with the young entrepreneur over capitalism
jokes.punchline: Jack's origin story as a capitalist is selling his own urine at Fenway Park specifically for fans to throw at Mickey Mantle — multi-layered absurdity (the product, the use, the target)
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a strong contender for the series. Jack's childhood entrepreneurship — selling urine for fans to throw at Mickey Mantle — is a perfectly constructed absurdist joke. Each element escalates: selling urine → to Fenway fans → for the specific purpose of throwing it → at a specific player. The pause after 'sell my urine' before the context reveal is great structure. Rivals the Field of Dreams joke for top spot in this episode.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Voters don't really pick the president. That's up to important people like corporations and celebrities.' / [earnestly] 'This year Jenna Maroney's picking the president.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains to a child how democracy works
jokes.punchline: His honest summary — corporations and celebrities pick the president — culminates in 'Jenna Maroney's picking the president' as the specific example, which is both darkly satirical and absurdly true within the episode
jokes.explanation: Sharp political satire — Jack's cynical civics lesson delivered earnestly to a child. The movement from 'corporations and celebrities' to 'Jenna Maroney' as the specific example is both funny and a genuine satirical point about celebrity influence in elections.

jokes.text: Girl decides to abandon business school savings for implants to be like Jenna: 'If I stop saving for business school and started saving for implants, I could be just like her. Thanks, sir!'
jokes.setup: Jack accidentally makes Jenna a role model to an impressionable young girl
jokes.punchline: The girl immediately pivots her life plan from education to cosmetic surgery, thanking Jack politely — the horror of the outcome vs. the chipper delivery
jokes.explanation: A darkly funny consequence joke — Jack's casual elevation of Jenna immediately corrupts a child. The 'Thanks, sir!' is a great kicker, implying she's genuinely grateful for this terrible life advice. Good structure.

jokes.text: 'Hey! I wasn't watching cute little kitten videos! I was watching pornography! Who put these sleepy kitten videos on here?'
jokes.setup: Tracy is discovered watching something on a screen
jokes.punchline: Tracy defensively announces he was watching porn — but then discovers someone replaced it with kitten videos without his knowledge, and he's upset about the switch
jokes.explanation: The reversal is good — Tracy volunteers that he was watching pornography (a defense of his dignity) only to discover he was actually watching kitten videos. His outrage at the swap is the real joke. The question 'who put these sleepy kitten videos on here?' implies a sinister kitten-video plotter, which is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Liz: 'You must have a lot of bad jokes about deceased celebrities just filling up your brain.' / Tracy: 'Yes, and they're pushing out important information. I don't know where I live, lady!'
jokes.setup: Liz notes Tracy has been storing up celebrity death jokes
jokes.punchline: Tracy confirms the jokes have displaced actual functional knowledge — he doesn't know his home address because it's been crowded out by too-soon jokes
jokes.explanation: Great escalation of the Tracy/Twitter ban joke. The cognitive displacement theory — jokes crowding out where he lives — is absurd but follows Tracy's internal logic. 'I don't know where I live, lady!' is an excellent kicker, delivered with genuine distress.

jokes.text: 'Ten, fifteen minutes. Less if I count genocides as celebrities.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks how quickly Tracy could get kicked off Twitter again
jokes.punchline: He can get banned faster if he's willing to make 'too soon' jokes about genocides — which he's apparently considered
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark joke. The implication that Tracy has been thinking about whether genocides count as celebrities for the purpose of his joke strategy is perfectly wrong. 'Less if I count genocides as celebrities' is economical and deeply quotable dark comedy. Near the top of the episode.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'I can't do that to my dear friend and co-worker Jenna Jameson.' / Liz: 'No, Tracy. Jenna Maroney.' / Tracy: 'Cool.'
jokes.setup: Tracy expresses loyalty to Jenna before hacking her account
jokes.punchline: He thinks Jenna's last name is Jameson (the porn star), and upon correction immediately drops all moral objection — 'Cool.' — suggesting his loyalty was entirely name-based
jokes.explanation: Tracy confusing Jenna Maroney with Jenna Jameson is good character comedy. The 'Cool.' upon correction is perfectly economical — it implies he was ONLY protecting Jenna Jameson, a completely different person he also apparently feels loyalty toward.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'How about "Me69"?' [as Jenna's password] / Liz: 'Yep!'
jokes.setup: They need to guess Jenna's password
jokes.punchline: Tracy's first guess is immediately correct — 'Me69' — the password perfectly encapsulates Jenna's narcissism and sexual brazenness
jokes.explanation: The immediate confirmation ('Yep!') is the joke — of course it's right, of course Jenna's password is 'Me69.' The specificity ('Me' not a name, the number) is perfect Jenna character comedy.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'No, I can say that word. I'm black.' / 'But Dick Clark wasn't!'
jokes.setup: Tracy is about to tweet something offensive from Jenna's account, Liz tries to stop him saying 'Tracy, no --'
jokes.punchline: Tracy clarifies his right to say a word based on race — but reveals the offensive tweet was about Dick Clark, not himself, raising the question of what he said about Dick Clark
jokes.explanation: Excellent, daring joke. Tracy claims a racial right to say a word — then reveals the issue isn't about himself but about Dick Clark (who died in 2012). The implication is that the 'word' he said about Clark was a racial epithet, which makes the joke simultaneously a commentary on racial language, a too-soon celebrity death joke, and a Tracy Jordan character joke all at once. 'But Dick Clark wasn't!' is one of the episode's most quotable and surprising lines. High economy, very high character integration.

jokes.text: Pete to Maria: 'I know it's the second time, but it's our last shot at feeling... this!' [presumably gestures grandly to the election broadcast or himself]
jokes.setup: Pete makes another desperate pitch to Maria
jokes.punchline: 'This!' with whatever gesture he makes — the grand romantic gesture deflated by Pete's inherent pathetic-ness
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe beat — Pete's romantic desperation is well-established but this particular moment is more setup than joke. Gets its comedy from cumulative character work rather than standalone craft.

jokes.text: Young cool guy appears to sweep Maria away: 'Hey, sugarlips. Let's make it like a black magazine and jet.' / [to Pete] 'What's up, guy?' / 'Thanks for keeping my lady warm while I turn on my hot tub with my phone.'
jokes.setup: Pete is about to make his move on Maria when a cooler version of himself appears
jokes.punchline: 'Let's make it like a black magazine and jet' (Jet magazine pun) + the casual 'What's up, guy?' dismissal of Pete + 'turn on my hot tub with my phone' (2012 smart home tech as cool flex) all compound
jokes.explanation: 'Let's make it like a black magazine and jet' is an inspired wordplay joke (Jet magazine + 'jet' as in leave). 'Turn on my hot tub with my phone' is perfectly 2012-era tech bro posturing. The whole character — alternate cool Pete — landing exactly when sad Pete thought he had a chance is great comedic timing.

jokes.text: Cool Pete's exit attempt: 'Well, well, well, well, well, well, well, well...' / [pause] 'Nope, it's too many wells. I'm gonna re-enter.'
jokes.setup: Cool Pete tries to make a dramatic entrance/exit with 'Well, well, well...'
jokes.punchline: He loses count, decides there were too many 'wells,' and physically exits to try again — acknowledging the performance failed mid-performance
jokes.explanation: Wonderful meta-comedy. Cool Pete self-critiques his own dramatic entrance mid-delivery, decides it failed technically, and literally re-enters. The moment is funny because: (1) he counted 'wells' while delivering them, (2) he decided 8 was too many, and (3) he treats this as a fixable problem rather than an embarrassment. 'I'm gonna re-enter' as a solution is inspired. High originality.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I stole a page from your playbook, Jack. I used Tracy. I committed cyber crime. I got Jenna kicked off Twitter before she could endorse Romney.' / Jack: 'Deviousness? I guess two can play at that game. Just like most games.'
jokes.setup: Liz confesses to manipulation
jokes.punchline: Jack's response to 'two can play at that game' is the pedantic observation 'just like most games' — technically true, completely deflating the idiom
jokes.explanation: Another solid Jack literalism/pedantry joke. 'Just like most games' is a perfectly timed qualifier — it's not wrong, it's just completely deflating. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: 'And now you're smiling because you're gonna try to tell me that this was your plan all along. I turned you into me, Lemon. That was my plan all along.'
jokes.setup: Liz preemptively scripts Jack's manipulative response
jokes.punchline: She performs his response for him before he can say it — exposing the predictability of his triumphalism
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Liz has learned Jack's patterns well enough to pre-empt them. Works as relationship comedy and character comedy simultaneously.

jokes.text: Jack: 'You sentimental, self-righteous, badger-faced shrew.' / Liz: 'Typical Lemon. You cynical, manipulative, cold-blooded Adonis.'
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz exchange affectionate insults after finding mutual respect
jokes.punchline: The exchange escalates to Jack calling Liz a 'badger-faced shrew' and Liz calling Jack a 'cold-blooded Adonis' — the compliment/insult hybrid is the joke, especially 'Adonis' as Liz's sincere-seeming descriptor for Jack
jokes.explanation: The insult exchange is well-crafted — 'badger-faced shrew' is a great compound insult, and 'cold-blooded Adonis' is a perfectly paradoxical description. 'Adonis' coming from Liz implies genuine physical admiration wrapped in an insult structure, which is funnier than a straight insult.

jokes.text: Jenna walks by drinking something, drips it on Liz: 'Mnh-mnh... Yours dripped on me, and now I'm drunk!'
jokes.setup: Jenna passes by mid-conversation between Jack and Liz
jokes.punchline: Jenna claims she got drunk from alcohol dripping onto her — implying such extreme sensitivity to alcohol (or such extreme current intoxication) that contact-dripping made her drunk
jokes.explanation: A good Jenna interruption gag — she passes through someone else's scene to deliver an absurd one-liner and exits. 'Now I'm drunk' from a drip implies she was already at maximum capacity. Works as a quick character beat.

jokes.text: Kenneth runs in having voted: 'I just voted! Doesn't it just fill you with hope like anything can happen?'
jokes.setup: Kenneth bursts in with electoral enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: After his entire plotline of being paralyzed by indecision and impossible ballot choices (clock hermit, Old Man Burkle marrying his daughter), he presents himself as a model civic participant
jokes.explanation: A warm callback to Kenneth's voting storyline. The joke is implicit — we know he voted randomly and chaotically based on Tracy's advice, yet he feels fully empowered. Works as a payoff beat more than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Pete responds to Kenneth's hope speech: 'All day, all night, baby.' — using Cool Pete's catchphrase
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks if Pete feels hope
jokes.punchline: Pete adopts Cool Pete's catchphrase, suggesting he's internalized something from the encounter
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to Cool Pete. Pete absorbing the catchphrase suggests he's taking on a piece of the confidence he witnessed. Works as an emotional payoff for the subplot. Economy is excellent — four words close the arc.

tmdb_overview: Realizing that Jenna could decide the Presidential election, Liz and Jack stage a debate to win her support and her followers. Kenneth turns to Tracy for advice on how to be an informed voter, while Pete tries to recreate the magic of the 2008 election.
insight: Two-part finale hits 82 jokes across network satire and character breakdown.
